newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka sets up human rights body to stem abuses.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka sets up human rights body to stem abuses.

text.p: Sri Lanka on Monday announced the creation of a permanent human rights commission with broad monitoring and investigative powers to help ensure widespread abuses of the recent past do not recur.

Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Gamini Lakshman Peiris said the five-member body would replace existing official human rights organisations and seek to rectify inadequacies in existing rights laws.

The commission will try to settle disputes before they go to court, advise the government on flaws in existing human rights protection laws, raise community awareness of rights issues and supervise conditions of those in detention, Peiris said.
"The protection of human rights is one of the most fundamental concerns of our government," Peiris told a news conference.

Sri Lanka has been accused of widespread rights abuses, with rights groups saying up to 60,000 people died or disappeared during a brutal crackdown by the former United National Party (UNP) government on a leftist youth insurgency in 1988-90.
Government forces fighting the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels in the island's north and east have also been accused of violations.
Gerard Peytrignet, head of of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Sri Lanka, said he hoped the new organisation would help improve the situation.
"The fact that we're present in the country shows the need for strengthening human rights protection," he told Reuters.

Political analyst Dayan Jayatilleka said the move was a positive step in improving the country's human rights situation, but that he had some reservations about the record of the current People's Alliance (PA) regime, in power since 1994.

"If you look at what has been happening on the ground over the last two years, where many political killings attributed to (government) supporters and members have gone unaddressed by the regime, one cannot help being a little cynical about the appointment of the commission," he told Reuters.
"I see a retrogression rather than an improvement over the past two years," he added.
Peiris said the composition of the commission would be a bipartisan exercise and reflect the country's ethnic balance.

"The composition of the commission will not be the sole prerogative of the government," he said. "We readily accepted an opposition suggestion that we should consult the leader of the opposition when members are appointed. We also want minority groups to be represented in the commission."
Jayatilleka, also the editor of the independent Lanka Guardian magazine, said the need for the concurrence of the now-opposition UNP in the commission's composition was a step forward.
"Particularly, President Chandrika Kumaratunga and the PA have been extremely confrontational towards the UNP and opposition leader Ranil Wickremesinghe," he said.

"If (the opposition's participation in the commission) actually materialises, it will be a step away from this dangerous confrontation, away from the high-octane rhetoric of the president to a saner consensual mode," he added.
